opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is simply incentives. AI isn't being developed by one actor who could decide to pause. It's being pushed forward by many companies, many countries, and huge numbers of researchers, each of whom sees real benefits: economic value, scientific progress, national security. Even if one group decides to slow down, the others have strong reasons to keep going. So it becomes a coordination problem, and historically, coordination problems on this scale are very hard to solve, especially when the technology is this general-purpose.

The second layer is that the knowledge is already out there. The core ideas, the scaling behavior of neural networks, the training techniques, a lot of it is published, open-sourced, or widely understood. Compute keeps getting cheaper. Once a technology reaches that point, you can't really put it back in the box. At most you can shape how fast it spreads and who has access to the frontier.

The third layer, which I think people sometimes underestimate, is that the demand is real. People genuinely find these systems useful. Students, programmers, doctors, researchers, they use them every day. When something delivers value to that many people, there's enormous bottom-up pressure for it to keep improving.

So when I say it can't be stopped, I don't mean we should be fatalistic. I mean the more productive question isn't "should we stop AI," but "given that it's going to keep advancing, how do we make it safe, make it trustworthy, and make sure the benefits are broadly shared?" That's where I think researchers and society can actually have leverage: alignment and safety research, evaluation, governance, and building norms before the capabilities outrun our ability to understand them.

r001.rationale: The response mentions competition among countries generally, but does not identify competition between the United States and China.

r002.rationale: It says companies see economic value in AI and have strong reasons to keep developing it, conveying their profit incentive.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's not really a technology question anymore, it's a game-theory question. If this were one lab in one country, you could imagine a regulator saying "pause," and maybe it would stick. But we're talking about dozens of companies and several governments, all of whom believe, correctly or not, that whoever is a year ahead on this gets to set the terms for everyone else. In that structure, unilateral restraint just hands the advantage to whoever didn't restrain themselves. So nobody stops, because stopping only works if everybody stops at the same time, and there's no mechanism to make that happen.

Then there's the economics. The marginal cost of running these models keeps falling, and the things they can do keep expanding. When something is simultaneously getting cheaper and more useful, demand for it doesn't go down. Every company that adopts it forces its competitors to adopt it. It's the same pattern we saw with electricity, with the internet, with smartphones. You can slow a wave like that at the margins, you can shape where it goes, but you can't un-ring the bell.

And the third piece, which I think people underestimate, is that the knowledge is already distributed. The core ideas are in papers anyone can read. Open-weight models are on laptops around the world. Even if the frontier labs all vanished tomorrow, you'd have thousands of smaller actors continuing from where they left off. It would be slower, but it wouldn't stop.

So when people ask me "should we stop," I actually think it's the wrong framing. The real question is: given that this is going to keep moving, what do we actually have leverage over? And I think we have quite a lot of leverage over direction, over who benefits, over what guardrails get built in. That's where I'd rather spend the energy, instead of on a pause that I don't think is achievable in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition among companies and several governments, but it does not identify competition between the United States and China.

r002.rationale: The response describes falling costs, growing usefulness, and competitive pressure to adopt AI, but does not clearly identify companies’ incentives to profit from AI.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very difficult to stop because there isn’t a single switch anyone can turn off. AI development is spread across countries, companies, universities, and individual researchers. Even if one group decides to pause, others still have strong incentives to keep going—whether that’s scientific curiosity, commercial opportunity, or competition.

And people can see useful applications. If AI helps someone do their work or solve a problem, they have a reason to keep improving it. That momentum is hard to reverse.

But I wouldn’t confuse “difficult to stop” with “impossible to influence.” We can still set limits on particular uses, require safety testing, and hold developers accountable. To me, the practical question is how we steer development so that the benefits don’t come at an unacceptable cost.

r001.rationale: It mentions countries and competition generally, but does not identify competition between the United States and China.

r002.rationale: It says companies have strong incentives to keep developing AI for commercial opportunity, communicating a profit motive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very difficult to stop because there isn’t one person or organization controlling it. Researchers want to solve problems, companies see opportunities, and governments see strategic value. Even if one group pauses, others still have reasons to keep going.

And AI already offers useful capabilities. Once people find that a tool helps them write code, analyze information, or do research, they want to improve it. That creates momentum.

But I’d distinguish between saying development is difficult to stop and saying we have no choices. We can still shape how these systems are tested, where they’re deployed, and who is accountable when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response mentions governments’ strategic value, but does not identify competition between the United States and China.

r002.rationale: It says companies see opportunities, but does not clearly identify profit as their incentive.
